newsitem.title: DUBAI: EU companies to meet in Saudi for Gulf trade talks.
newsitem.headline: EU companies to meet in Saudi for Gulf trade talks.

text.p: Gulf Arab countries hope increased European investment and trade will result from talks this week with more than 100 European companies in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Some 120 European companies are attending the three-day "GCC-EU Enterprise 1997" meeting, due to start on Tuesday and backed by the European Commission, the organisers said.
They are hoping to break new investment ground in the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), uncharted territory for many of them.
The GCC is an alliance of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar and Oman, whose members are trying to lure foreign investment and diversify their oil-run economies.

"The aim of the conference is very much to encourage partnership between companies from Europe and possible joint venture partners in this region," Richard Northern, Britain's commercial attache in Riyadh, told Reuters.
"It is a very constructive way forward in evolving the trade relationship between the two sides," he said.
The GCC exports some $22 billion worth of goods, mostly oil, to the EU but has a trade deficit of $15 billion with Europe.
While firms from all Gulf Arab states will attend, delegates said the focus would be on regional powerhouse Saudi Arabia.
"Even though the conference doesn't just cover Saudi firms but the GCC as a whole, the majority of companies are Saudi," said Miriam Teuwen, national counsellor for the German team.
The German delegation is the largest, with 26 small and mid-sized firms, 60 percent of them from eastern Germany.

"For most of the companies it is their first exposure to Saudi Arabia. About 60 percent of the companies (from sectors such as food to construction and chemicals) have never been to Saudi Arabia before," said Teuwen.

According to German embassy figures, bilateral trade between Germany and Saudi Arabia was around 4.8 billion marks ($2.8 billion) in 1995, down from 5.7 billion marks in 1994. In the first nine months of 1996 it stood at 3.7 billion marks.
Italy's economic and commercial counsellor in Riyadh Luigi DeChiara said his country's delegation was the third largest after Germany and France, with 15 firms participating.
He said Italy was among Riyadh's top five trade partners, with Italian exports including food, fashion and machinery.
"The bilateral trade balance for 1996 was a little bit more than $4 billion," DeChiara said, adding that trade last year increased by about 14 percent.
He said the balance was slightly in favour of Saudi Arabia, whose exports to Italy were worth slightly over $2 billion.

Northern said European firms did not appear to be deterred by a Saudi law requiring a Saudi partner to control at least 51 percent of every joint venture. "Once the right partner and project has been identified, the precise breakdown of shareholding and ownership is not usually an obstacle," he said.
"Our bilateral trade in merchandise exports and visible goods in 1996 was a record. It went up 51 percent over the total for 1995 to reach almost 2.5 billion pounds ($4.1 billion)."
That meant Saudi Arabia was Britain's 13th largest export market, he said, adding that the balance was in Britain's favour.
